album: Homecoming: Live at the Village Vanguard
label: Columbia
rationale: Consensus: AllMusic rates the album 4.5/5 (Scott Yanow's review, tabulated on the album article and carried on AllMusic's own page, S1 and S2), the jazz.com Dozens entry scores it 95/100 (S5) and its separate 'Round Midnight review 92/100 (S6), and the record opens Columbia's seven-CD Complete Columbia Albums retrospective of Gordon's 1976-80 run (S9) — three independent traditions of listing, rating, and anthologising the same set. Defining statement: this is the night Dexter Gordon came home. He had left the United States in 1962 for Europe and Copenhagen, and the December 1976 week at the Village Vanguard was his return engagement, recorded and released under the title the occasion gave it (S1, S5). It is also, on the jazz.com reading, the moment the jazz world publicly re-valued a career that had run from swing through bop to hard bop (S5). Lineage: Gordon played the week in front of Woody Shaw's working quintet, with Louis Hayes on drums (S5), which puts a 1940s founding bopper inside the strongest young acoustic band of the mid-1970s — the exact bridge this canon is built to record. Session gravity: Shaw, Ronnie Mathews, Stafford James and Louis Hayes are a working band, not a pickup rhythm section, and the ten tracks run long the way a club set runs long. Discovery value: 'Gingerbread Boy', 'Little Red's Fantasy', 'In Case You Haven't Heard', 'Fenja' and 'Backstairs' are not the standards a newcomer has already heard, and the eleven-to-fourteen-minute performances let a listener hear how a great bop improviser builds over a long arc. Case against: it is a live double LP with no studio economy, the sound is a club recording, and the canon already holds four of Gordon's 1960s studio records — the argument for this one has to be the homecoming and the band, not the repertoire.

personnel_record.notes: Two consecutive nights at the Village Vanguard, December 11 and 12, 1976. No source consulted splits the ten tracks between the two dates — both AllMusic and JazzDiscography give the pair of dates for the whole run — so every track carries session_date null rather than an inferred assignment, and the album is marked multi_session with both dates at block level. The quintet is identical on every track in all four personnel sources; no per-track substitution is documented. Two credit conflicts are preserved rather than smoothed: AllMusic's credits tab lists Woody Shaw additionally under 'Sax (Tenor)' (S2), contradicted by S1, S3 and S4, and read here as an AllMusic error; the Discogs submission also carries a 'Saxophone — Rene McLean' credit with no track, role position or instrument specified (S3), which no other source corroborates and which the taxonomy cannot express without inventing an instrument — so McLean is recorded here as a flagged conflict, not as personnel. Recording engineer: Malcolm Addey, credited as Engineer, Mixed By and Recorded By (S2, S3); remote recording facilities were supplied by Kaleb Sound (S3), and mixing and mastering took place at CBS Recording Studios, New York (S3) — a post-production location, not a recording site. The CD reissue adds 'Fried Bananas' and 'Body and Soul' from the same engagement; both are flagged bonus.

ballot.album: Dexter Gordon — Homecoming: Live at the Village Vanguard (1976)

scope_check.boundary_note: Recorded December 11–12, 1976 and first released in 1977; both dates are within the window. The 1973–1985 continuity boundary applies, but this acoustic Gordon–Shaw quintet directly extends the bebop and post-bop lineage rather than introducing an electric-rock or other stylistic departure.

ballot.case_for: This is a defining comeback document: Gordon's December 1976 Village Vanguard engagement connects a founding bebopper with Woody Shaw's working acoustic band, making the continuity between generations audible rather than merely historical (S4–S6). Shaw, Ronnie Mathews, Stafford James and Louis Hayes supply substantial session gravity, while their original compositions and extended performances offer discovery beyond a familiar standards program (S1, S3–S5). AllMusic's 4.5/5 rating and jazz.com's enthusiastic assessments support its musical standing, and Jazzwise identifies it as the opening document of Columbia's retrospective of Gordon's 1976–80 period (S2, S5, S6, S9).
ballot.case_against: The original eight-track double LP sustains roughly 102 minutes of extended performances, creating a genuine discovery trade-off: immersive club storytelling can also mean fatigue and less concentrated impact than a tightly shaped album (S1, S3, S4). Its historical occasion establishes importance more securely than the dossier establishes downstream musical influence, so the homecoming narrative should not substitute for an album-level canonical case. Consensus evidence is narrower than advertised: Wikipedia repeats AllMusic, the two jazz.com assessments share an outlet, and opening a chronological complete-albums box is weaker evidence of selective canonization than an independent core-collection citation.
ballot.disagreement: Reference 1 judges the continuity test decisively passed and the musical and historical evidence overwhelming enough for consensus_core; Reference 2 favors contested, emphasizing the rubric's 1973+ default, double-LP sprawl and narrower-than-claimed consensus. Both rate the priority strong and agree that the acoustic lineage is clear. Reference 1 also invokes Gordon's existing representation as a reservation; Reference 2 correctly rejects artist concentration as an objection under the rubric.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John give this strong-priority contested candidate a focused listening review, weighing its Gordon–Shaw continuity and live storytelling against its length and limited independent canon-list evidence.
